#3927. Phasmophobia players raise over $230,000 for heart charity, more than double last year's total

The Phasmophobia community has raised more than $230,000 (around £173,000) for the American Heart Association, more than doubling last year's total.

Developer Kinetic Games announced the final figure for this year's Ghost Hunts for Hearts event on 6th November. The charity drive ran from 26th October to 2nd November, and more than 500 streamers signed up to take part. That's the biggest turnout yet for a creator fundraiser run by Heart Liive, the American Heart Association's streaming initiative.

Last year's event raised a little over $100,000.

Congratulations, Ghost Hunters, you've surpassed the community target and raised over $200,000 for our friends at @Heart_Liive!Your kindness and generosity will not go unrewarded, log in to Phasmophobia before the 15th November to claim the Animated AHA Advocate ID Card &… pic.twitter.com/KFQKaqXNCl

Streamers who fundraised could hand out an event-exclusive Advocate ID Card and Badge to their viewers as a Twitch Drop. Kinetic set a target of $200,000 at the start of the week, and once players sailed past it, an animated version of the card and badge set unlocked for all.

"The Phasmophobia community never fails to amaze us, and this year they've outdone themselves," said Tom Dent, lead social media and player experience manager at Kinetic Games. "Thank you to every streamer, viewer and player who took part."

Phasmophobia launched in Early Access in September 2020, and sends teams of up to four players into haunted locations to gather evidence of what's lurking there.

The studio also launched a publishing arm, Kinetic Publishing, earlier this year. Its first game, the starship job simulator Contact Protocol, is due out in spring 2027.

Phasmophobia is available in Early Access on Steam, PS5, PS VR2, and Xbox Series X/S. It's also coming to Nintendo Switch 2, although we still don't quite know when.

Earlier this year, Kinetic Games confirmed Phasmophobia's 1.0 launch had slipped from this year into 2027, as the studio said it was prioritising quality over speed following a rocky reception to its Player Character Update. The studio ended up apologising to players for issues with the long-awaited update, admitting it "missed the mark" and "didn't deliver on our promises to you".

#3926. Avengers: Doomsday has a chance to right the wrongs of Captain America: Brave New World and do Sam Wilson's Cap justice

On the road to Avengers: Doomsday, we revisit Multiverse Saga misfire Captain America: Brave New World

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite some four years of hype for a Sam Wilson solo movie, Captain America: Brave New World quietly came and went. Following the events of The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, the movie saw Anthony Mackie's Wilson take on the Captain America mantle, with Joaquin Torres (Danny Ramirez) as his trusty Falcon. Though it fared well at the box office, the film ultimately suffers from something I call re-shoot-itus, and it's not entirely difficult to see what was rewritten or reshot... which ultimately made for a pretty disjointed-feeling two-hour romp that felt a bit disconnected from the MCU.

Critiques aside, Sam Wilson finally gets to shine as Cap, and he's a naturally funny, take-no-crap hero who, despite being the literal face of the country, still doesn't trust authority or the government at all, for that matter. He butts heads with President Thadeus Ross, played by Harrison Ford in his one and only Marvel stint, and the final battle is a Hulk vs. Cap showdown in front of the freakin' White House.

Welcome to Road to Doomsday, GamesRadar+'s weekly MCU rewatch series. Over 15 weeks, we'll be revisiting each Marvel movie and TV show on Disney's list of essential movies to watch ahead of Avengers: Doomsday, sharing our thoughts upon rewatching and deciphering what we can learn about the next Marvel mega-event from each entry. Why not relive some MCU highlights and watch along with us?

As we gear up for Avengers: Doomsday (which is somehow just one month away), Brave New World is definitely worth a revisit – especially since, at least judging by the trailers and Mackie's recent press tour, the newest Avengers movie will let Sam Wilson shine as a leader amongst the Avengers... as well as every other Marvel superhero known to man (Earth-616 or otherwise) that seems to be making an appearance.

Sam does save the world in Brave New World, and he does quite a bit of it alone after Torres is injured during a mid-air fight after Samuel Sterns, aka the Leader, mind-controls two American fighter pilots and makes them crash. That's sort of what makes the whole movie for me: director Julius Onah (and the writing team consisting of Rob Edwards, Malcolm Spellman, Dalan Musson, and Peter Glanz) wanted to make sure that Sam had his big solo hero moment. At the end of the film, Sam proves to the country, his main naysayer Thaddeus Ross, and MCU fans (if you want to get meta about it) that he knows how to wield the hell out of that shield.

And you know what? One of the best things about Sam Wilson is that he simply doesn't want to be. He isn't deterred by Ross saying this, either: "You're right," Sam replies. "I'm not." The clash of egos is ultimately what propels the film forward: Ross invites Sam to the White House, but he won't go unless he can bring American hero Isaiah Bradley, whom Ross ultimately doesn't trust. While there, Ross asks Sam to help reform the Avengers, which Sam more or less shuts down. But it gets worse: during a special presentation for world leaders about newly discovered adamantium, a song begins to play and Bradley, alongside a few other men, begins shooting at the President.

It's clear to Sam, Torres, and the audience that Bradley was momentarily 'possessed' in an activated sleeper-cell kind of situation. Ross, of course, doesn't believe this... but he's got some secrets of his own. Sam manages to figure out that Samuel Sterns has been masterminding all of this in an attempt to take revenge against Ross, who promised to release Sterns from prison in exchange for the production of life-saving pills that are meant to keep Ross's heart from failing. Ross ultimately refused to release Sterns out of fear that he would stop making the pills, so Sterns decided to use his freaky deaky mind powers to ruin Ross's life from behind bars. Oh, and there's also the fact that the pills make him turn into the Hulk. But we'll get to that in a moment.

Sam Wilson finally gets to shine as Cap, and he's a naturally funny, take-no-crap hero who still doesn't trust authority

I'll level with you: we probably won't revisit any of this in Avengers: Doomsday, and if the President of the United States does show up, it won't be Thaddeus Ross (on account of the whole Hulk and illegal deal with Sterns thing). What we will revisit, however, is the Captain America: Brave New World post-credits scene. The scene gave us our biggest and clearest clue to the plot of Doomsday well before the Russos confirmed that incursions would plague Earth-616 in Doomsday, and before we even knew that the upcoming film was closely following the Jonathan Hickman Avengers run.

In the post-credits scene, Sam goes to visit Sterns. Sterns, who is a super-genius who can predict infinite outcomes with his intelligence (and big, gross oversized brain that makes his skull look like mashed potatoes), warns Sam about a threat... a multiversal threat. "We share the same world, don't we, this world that you will die to save," Sterns says... but you'll have to rewatch the movie in order to hear the rest. It's no fun (nor does it get you hyped for Avengers: Doomsday) if I just type out the entire thing.

When Harrison Ford was announced as Red Hulk at San Diego Comic-Con, he not only ran around on stage with Anthony Mackie, but he also... pretended to Hulk out on stage. They got Han Solo and Indiana Jones to growl like the Incredible Hulk. That was all the promo I needed to get me hyped for Brave New World, personally.

Anything can happen in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (like Wanda Maximoff coming back from the dead, or Frank Castle experiencing actual unbridled joy), so who's to say we won't see Red Hulk? It may not be Harrison Ford's Red Hulk (as he simply responded 'no' when asked if he would be in another Marvel movie), but it could be one from another universe. It's also worth noting that, as the Avengers: Endgame Encore post-credits scenes revealed, OG Hulk Bruce Banner has been captured by Doctor Doom. Therefore, the Avengers don't have a Hulk on their team to help them defeat Doom.

The fan theory is that Sam visits Ross in prison and recruits him to help them in their race to save the entire galaxy as they know it, and I'd say it's pretty plausible. Though Thaddeus Ross/Red Hulk isn't in the Hickman Avengers comics (and therefore isn't around to help them save the world), it looks like Doomsday is taking several detours from the comics... so why not add a Red Hulk?

Black Panther: Wakanda Forever is still Marvel's best passing of the torch – so I hope Shuri gets to shine in Avengers: Doomsday

Because Avengers: Doomsday is an ultimate team-up, I'm excited to watch Sam Wilson to plain ol' interact with the other heroes. We already know that Namor is probably going to hit on Sue Storm, so why not add Yelena and Sam having the ultimate unimpressed sass-off? It'll also just be super fun to watch him face off against Doctor Doom, and maybe even make a comment about that rather interesting accent.

Captain America: Brave New World is available to stream now on Disney Plus, ahead of the release of Avengers: Doomsday on December 18.

Look ahead with our list of upcoming Marvel movies and check out how to watch the Marvel movies in order ahead of your next re-watch. See you next week as we revisit Deadpool & Wolverine.

#3925. Keeping hold of Company of Heroes was essential for Relic to leave Sega, Relic CEO says – "Without it we would have been a dead studio"

In the nearly 30 years since they opened their doors, Relic have been an enormously influential studio. Responsible for lauded RTS series Homeworld, Dawn of War, and Company of Heroes, they also dabbled in other genres with third-person shooter The Outfit and the original Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine. Yet, despite this history, in 2024, when Relic were negotiating their sale from Sega to UK investment firm Emona Capita, CEO Justin Dowdeswell knew the rights to Company of Heroes had to be part of the deal. "Without it we would have been a dead studio," he tells me.

Without naming names Dowdeswell points out that there are "numerous examples" of studios that weren't able to survive on their name alone. Not only did Relic need the ability to make more games in the series that they were known for, but they also needed the income from back catalogue sales a series like Company of Heroes provides.

Dowdeswell joined Relic shortly after Sega acquired the studio in 2013. This was in the immediate aftermath of publisher THQ's bankruptcy auction, where studios and franchises were sold off to the highest bidder. While Sega bought the studio, they didn't buy the licenses to everything Relic had created. "The other games that Relic made – Homeworld, Impossible Creatures, The Outfit... formative games in many people's memory – they were all split up, scattered," Dowdeswell says. "I think that was... I won't say a tragedy, but it's unfortunate because Relic is the home of those games. It would have been great for them to stay with the studio."

Just as a hint of the messy history of acquisitions and auctions: this year we see Dawn of War 4 coming from studio King Art Games and published by Deep Silver. Deep Silver are a subdivision of Plaion, formerly called Koch Media, which was acquired by Embracer Group back when they were called THQ Nordic. Not that they were actually the THQ that originally published Relic's Dawn of War, Nordic Games renamed themselves THQ Nordic after they bought the THQ trademark at auction.

As for Homeworld, Borderlands developer Gearbox picked up the license to the sci-fi RTS in the bankruptcy auction, then contracted Blackbird Interactive's support on the remasters, before handing the latter lead development on Homeworld 3. That chain of events does have a more clear throughline to Relic's past however, as Blackbird was created by two of Relic's co-founders Rob Cunningham and Jon Aaron Kambeitz. (Speaking of studios struggling without the series they made their name with, Blackbird was on the verge of bankruptcy before Gearbox got in touch with the Homeworld work. So we very nearly existed in a world where they never got to make the brilliant Homeworld: Deserts of Kharak and Hardspace Shipbreaker.)

None of this is intended to be a knock on Dawn of War 4. From what I've played it's a very good Warhammer 40K RTS, if it perhaps sticks a little closely to the model laid down by Relic's original. What do I know, though, talking about their own games, Dowdeswell tells me that while "one of the messages to the studio is we can't just make [the same] things that we made 20 years ago and hope it goes well", re-releasing the 20-year-old Dawn of War sold very well for Relic and netted the team some very positive reviews on Steam. "There's a bit of a paradox there," he adds"

Anyway, this is all getting side-tracked. Back to holding onto Company of Heroes when separating from Sega. "Fighting for Company of Heroes when leaving Sega was crucial because I already lamented the fact that the other games didn't come with Relic," Dowdeswell says. "I couldn't really imagine a Relic where none of the games that the studio has made and was known for were any longer part of it."

Relic and new owner UK investment firm Emona Capital LLP were able to negotiate Company of Heroes as part of the sale from Sega and since then the studio has spent the past two years focusing largely on supporting the WW2 RTS and restoring their back catalogue. The most recent update is the massive 3.0 patch to mark the series' 20th anniversary. Which, among many changes, overhauls the Mediterranean-set RTS game's special effects, audio systems, NPC AI, and makes significant changes to the singleplayer grand strategy-inspired Italy campaign, as well as adding a whole set of autumn and winter-themed assets for community map makers. They've also released a series of DLCs adding new factions to Company of Heroes 3's skirmishes and multiplayer, re-released Dawn of War with a definitive edition and announced they're doing the same for the original Company of Heroes, along with Blackbird Interactive's help. Dowdeswell says foundation building masks a lot of the work going on behind the scenes: "We now self-publish all of this," he explains. "There were a number of things that we had to learn, skills we had to develop, capacity and capability that we had to build at the studio very, very quickly."

I ask if it was always the plan to focus on their back catalogue, or if they had plans to release new games. Dowdeswell says spending four years quietly working on a new game wasn't an option: "It's almost impossible to do it that way because of the current climate in the industry. We don't have a financial safety net." Though, the team do have larger ambitions. "We want to make new games, we want to provide a modern Relic game," Dowdeswell says. "That ambition to re-establish Relic as an innovator in this strategy space is a big part of what drives our creative direction on new games." Focusing on updating Company of Heroes 3, releasing DLC for the game, and making definitive editions of Dawn of War and the original Company of Heroes is what gets the studio to the place it can make a new game.

However, Dowdeswell resists any framing of Relic's work on Company of Heroes 3 as spinning their wheels or resting on their laurels while working toward a new game. He argues the game "sits in between" Relic's past and its future: "It's an established game that came out three years ago, but it's also a way for us to take some chances, experiment a little bit, and while doing that staying really closely connected to the players, That's what the idea was behind the updates because it was a way to have very quick iterations and touch points with players and provide, honestly, a way for us to fund everything in the future."

As to what Relic is making next, Dowdeswell wouldn't say. Though, he revealed trying genres besides real-time strategy was "almost a certainty", before adding "I don't think it's going to be a vast departure for where we are, so it will still be strategic gameplay. We're not going to go build a racer."

#3924. 'PS5 Pro Is Not Powerful Enough to Run GTA 6 at 60fps': Rockstar Explains Frame Rate Decision

I’ve played GTA 6 on PS5 Pro for over 150 hours and it’s a remarkable experience. You can read my review through here.

This is the densest open world ever designed. The sheer amount of art assets on screen at any given time is simply unprecedented.

There is a downside to all the detail, though: the Rockstar release bucks contemporary console trends and runs at 30fps, without compromise. There’s no Performance option, even on Sony’s most powerful platform, which will run you $900 these days.

I spoke to Rockstar’s Marc Chambers, the man in charge of Technology Production to try to understand why.

“The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the games visual fidelity,” he said.

“While the PS5 Pro’s central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it’s not powerful enough to run the game’s complex simulation at higher frame rates.”

In other words, it’s as many already predicted: GTA 6’s performance is limited by its robust CPU demands.

Chambers continued: “GTA 6 pushes the current-generation console hardware to its absolute limits. The complexity of simulating and rendering the environments and inhabitants in a world the scale of Leonida, while maintaining the density, visual fidelity, and player agency we envisaged, places extraordinary demands on the hardware. Bringing all of these systems together and completing the required work for every frame is only just possible within a ~33ms frame budget.”

The remarkable thing to me is, despite the drop to 30fps, I found the game to feel very responsive overall. Aiming is snappy and movement feels less cumbersome than in past Rockstar releases, like Red Dead Redemption 2.

Rockstar’s Vice President of Technology David Hynd told me that the team was able to remove one full frame of delay compared to past titles.

“The input controller is sampled as late as possible during the game update. As a consequence, the game is updated with the most recent input data and we minimise the time between pressing a button and seeing the results on screen,” he said.

You really do feel this: I was switching between GTA 6 and several other 60fps PS5 games during the review process, and while the frame rate difference was obvious to my eyes, it didn’t feel as dramatic as I’d expected.

“For our game mechanics, we ensured that we stripped as much ‘dead space’ out of the start of our animations as possible,” Hynd continued. “And ensured that we could seamlessly interrupt them as early as was practical.”

There are still moments where GTA 6 feels clumsy, but it’s a marked improvement in playability compared to past games, despite the drop in frame rate.

Overall, I think Rockstar made the right decision.

The decision to lock gameplay at 30fps is objectively disappointing, but on a PS5 Pro the performance is smooth throughout, and the controller response is surprisingly good.

With the sheer amount of art assets on the screen at any given time, I think it would have been a shame to see Rockstar compromise its vision.

This is the most immersive open world ever made, and I think it’s clear the team has put as much thought as possible into making sure it feels smooth and responsive at 30fps.

#3923. Ocarina of Time remake datamine suggests Master Quest is on the way

Ocarina of Time's notoriously tricky Master Quest mode could be making a comeback in the new remake.

Dataminer MrCheeze shared a list of strings from the remake's files on Bluesky, several of which tie the tag "MQ" to dungeons like Dodongo's Cavern.

In a follow-up, as spotted by TheGamer, they pointed to further entries, including "HasMQ", "IsMQModeExist", "NewGameMQ", and "ReleaseMQ".

Fellow dataminer OatmealDome added on Twitter/X that the mode will be unlocked by owning DLC, rather than arriving in an update, though "the data is incomplete". "I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly)," they said.

If you've not played it, Master Quest is a remixed version of Ocarina of Time with rearranged dungeons and tougher puzzles. It first appeared as a bonus disc on GameCube, then came back in 2011's Ocarina of Time 3D, which unlocked it after you finished the main game. That version also mirrored the whole world, which matches what OatmealDome has found, and had enemies deal double damage.

[Ocarina of Time] #ootspoilersThere is data in the game files for Master Quest. It will be unlocked by *owning DLC* - it is not just an update.The data is incomplete, but I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly).

As with any datamine, there's no guarantee it'll ever see the light of day. Nintendo hasn't announced any DLC for the remake, and it's not clear whether Master Quest would be free, like it was on 3DS, or paid.

The Ocarina of Time remake launched on Switch 2 on 5th November. Donlan called the new version an "astonishing remake" in his five-star Eurogamer Ocarina of Time review.

#3922. Casualties: Unknown is a total pain simulator that makes other survival games seem like massive cowards

Content warning for discussion of extreme violence and self-harm.

You haven't died in a videogame till you've died in Casualties: Unknown, a profoundly unwholesome cousin of Spelunky that simulates injury, infection and sensory distress with the same gusto Crusader Kings 3 reserves for papal politics. This is an intricate and imaginative celebration of pain - not merely an exacting survival game full of gauges to manage, but a laboratory study of just how many ways an animal body can feel, before it finally gives up the ghost.

I am one of a million canine hominids, created to undergo spectacular indignities by vicious human scientists, in a universe of suffering that spans several games from developer Orsoniks. I am the sorrowing vat-grown pup of a conclave of star-faring Dr Moreaus. My task is to collect... something, some gadget of great importance, from a cave on a deathly planet, located beneath three kilometres of booby-trapped and infested, poisonous and hateful rock.

Currently, I am trying to burrow into a sealed titanium drop pod with my bare paws, so that I can sleep somewhere warm. Too warm, in fact. The drop pod heaters feel like they were vindictively designed to discourage occupants from lingering, but I'm finding that dehydration is easier to address than hypothermia - there are pools of groundwater around that harbour only a slight risk of "minorly" fouling my intestines. So into the pod we go. After ripping away a layer of rubber, I smash some glass panes and promptly step in the fragments.

My computer screams, a hideous jangle of chords and static. The interface becomes a fritzing, flexing sphincter of pinks and reds. My punctured dogsbody flops and writhes, spurting yellow fluids and gobs of unintelligible text, ignoring my button inputs. They are my avatar no longer. They have been reduced to a squirming facet of the simulation's agony.

I gawp in guilt and terror at the status bar, now jammed with pulsing icons, then switch to my health display and determine that I am "bleeding catastrophically" from my right hind paw. I need to bandage that paw quickly. But first, I need to remove the glass. This takes the form of a 'minigame' in which I guide a shaking clawed hand with the cursor, hauling out shards even as my poor character threatens to pass out from the ordeal.

I've got two of five shards out when the earthquake kicks in. Already doubled over and delirious, my pioneering pooch is launched over the nearest cliff. They fall about 50 feet, rag-dolling off crags with a concussive whump, till they smash into a flooded wooden platform. The anatomical diagram on the health screen lights up like a wickerman. I don't appear to have broken any bones, but everything is hurting. What's more, I am soaking wet and hypothermia is taking hold, stretching blue veins through the clenching colours of my pain. The screen begins to look like some exotic, putrid flower.

Wringing my hands, I allow my mutant mutt about 10 seconds to recover from the shock of the fall, then open the health screen again and slowly tug out the last three shards of glass. It's actually easier than before, but not for the happiest of reasons: landing on my head appears to have numbed my senses. There will be longer term consequences, probably. Now I just have to bind the wound… except that I must have dropped my roll of gauze, while tumbling through the abyss. With sirens still flashing on the HUD, I peer about for a cave plant or other source of crafting materials. On the other side of the platform, I spy the corpse of another pitiful lab experiment. Perhaps there's a bandage in that huddle of clothes?

I hoist my sagging and babbling starpup to their feet, and limp over to investigate. Then I step on a pressure plate, and a six foot blade shoots up through my left thigh.

The screen is almost obliterated by crimson snow. The noise is... indescribable. I open the health screen again to assess the damage but I can't, because my dogperson has fallen into utter derangement. They want to be rid of their too-fruitful arteries, their stinking yellow blood. The clawed hand reappears, and I am forced to rake my own torso with it to regain access to the controls.

I am now gushing my life out from head to foot. Going by my plummeting heart rate, I have about 30 seconds to burn before I lose consciousness forever. I see no means of recovery, and I can't bear to watch my character bleed out. So instead, I detonate the chip embedded in their brain - the same chip responsible for the interface's rash of icons and warnings. According to the subsequent mission report print-out, my canine pioneer was feeling "dejected" when their head exploded.

The worst thing about the scenario I've just recalled is that it represents Casualties: Unknown at its least punishing. All of the above took place in the first of the game's 11 biomes - each procedurally generated, and 300 metres high - on the default "Tough" run setting. Resources are more plentiful up here, while active threats are fewer. There is scope to faff about and prepare - gathering plant matter for a crude woven bag, so I don't have to carry everything in my hands or mouth or tuck it into the folds of my body. There is time to crack open supply crates, and craft an implement of some kind.

The main danger, traps aside, is falling. Casualties: Unknown's terrain generator is not your pal. As regards the opening couple of biomes, at least, it works like a broken muck spreader, ejecting a mix of filthy clogs and particles that snag your jumps and often oblige you to dig through rock and gravel. You'll frequently be doing that in the dark, and even the smallest of exertions takes a perceptible toll – whimpers of effort, wheezing breath, double vision. The one major consolation is that you can wall-jump and slide down surfaces, a mocking touch of Prince of Persia.

Still, further down is where life gets truly unpleasant. There are sonic traps in certain biomes that cause brain damage and massive hemorrhaging. There are vast, rumbling insects you simply cannot afford to get close to, because they are guaranteed to bite off a limb. And the absolutely dreadful thing about that is that it won't necessarily end your run: given a tourniquet and antibiotics, you may yet pull through. Perhaps you'll find or craft a prosthetic. The game's characters are, in general, astonishingly tough for all their immense capacity for anguish.

Casualties: Unknown is a brilliant and unusual piece of design, uninhibited by any commercialised and sanitary notions of 'fun' and 'difficulty'. It's committed to recreating the surge of sensation through flesh. There's something intrinsically vital about this. Like Project Citadel, perhaps, its extravaganzas of torment are about feeling more present and alive in a twisted world, more in control. I'm not the writer to discuss this, and I know little about the developer's circumstances, but it feels like an exploration of trans survival in the face of a brutalising biopolitical regime: the online wiki notes that the game's zoomorphic Experiments or "Expies" have their own ideas about gender, though I'm finding it tricky to distinguish those accounts from the categorisations of the evidently unfriendly boffins who engineered them.

I would like to get to the bottom of things. I would like to find that goddamn gadget. I would like to return to the surface and massacre the bastards who sent me down here. Still, I'm not sure I have the willpower to witness everything my avatar might have to endure: barotrauma, sepsis, strokes, ruptured ears, hallucinations... As I've hopefully made clear throughout this piece, it remains an open question as to whether I am them, or simply one of their human tormentors. You can read more on Steam and Itch.

#3921. Three Big Takeaways From Digital Foundry's GTA 6 Analysis For Xbox Series X|S

The good folks over at Digital Foundry have been sharing their deep dive analysis on the Xbox Series X/S versions of GTA 6 today, presented in the form of a 23-minute video on YouTube, and a separate article over on their website.

Feature GTA 6: PS5 vs PS5 Pro, Xbox Series X and Series S: Which Console Plays Best?

Digital FoundryResolution, performance and visual settings compared.

Looking at both of these, there's a ton of interesting information that's shared about the two Xbox versions of the game, so we thought we'd provide a quick summary of what they think about GTA 6 on Xbox Series X and S.

This is just a summary though, and there's way more context and detail in the video at the bottom of this article.

Digital Foundry reckons that the Xbox Series X version of GTA 6 is a great-looking game for the most part, highlighting things like lighting, reflections and even the incredible hair system, while also pointing out minor downsides such as missing shadows and occasionally blurry appearances. They also reckon that the frame rate generally maintains its 30FPS target, but will slip in busy situations like chases and explosions.

"Generally speaking, the game acquits itself quite well on Microsoft's senior current-gen console. Visual settings seem pretty solid across the board."

The Xbox Series S version is also said to be pretty fantastic in the visual department, retaining the core features that make GTA 6 such a great game visually. It's the frame rate that bothers DF the most, as it's much more variable and prone to falling below its 30FPS target. That said, it appears to hover around 25-30FPS for the most part.

"Series S offers the loosest 30fps lock, with large portions of the game playing out at frame-rates from the mid to high 20s. Again, it's possible to depress the frame-rate to around 20fps with vehicular destruction. The other consoles do a credible job of hitting 30fps, but Series S often lies in a 25-30fps no-man's-land."

If you're wondering which console is the absolute best to play GTA 6 on, it's unsurprisingly the PS5 Pro. Nevertheless, Digital Foundry says that both the Xbox Series X and the PS5 versions "look and play well" despite their softer image, while the Xbox Series S version is the "hardest to recommend" despite its impressive visuals.

"In terms of visual features and performance, the PS5 Pro version is the best option available, with solid frame-rates, 4K-like image quality and a noticeable visual upgrade thanks to ray-traced shadows. However, the game looks and plays well on base PS5 and Xbox Series X as well, despite occasional minor frame-rate drops during regular play and a softer 1440p image. The Series S version of the game is the hardest to recommend, with consistent frame-rate drops to the mid-20s, a 1080p output resolution and a long list of visual cutbacks, though the overall character of the game's visuals still shines through."

Both the video and the website article are totally different from each other, so it's worth watching / reading the pair of them and getting a better idea of how GTA 6 fares across both Xbox consoles (and PS5 for that matter).

In my experience, I've found GTA 6 to be fantastic on Xbox Series X across the board for the most part, and while the Series S version is clearly a little more unstable, I'd wager that most players will still be perfectly happy with it.

#3920. COD: Modern Warfare 4 gets a surprisingly sudden free trial, so you can see what the game's extraction mode DMZ is like

Activision has released the first trial for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's extraction mode DMZ. The trial is available across PC (Steam / Battlenet), PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S until Wednesday, 11th November.

The free trial only includes access to DMZ and no other part of Modern Warfare 4, such as multiplayer or the campaign. And while it's not uncommon for Call of Duty titles to make some of their modes available for free for a limited time, the timing of this DMZ taster is notable.

DMZ launched days before Modern Warfare 4's 23rd October release date, meaning this first trial has arrived just two weeks after the game's full launch. By comparison, Black Ops 7's Endgame mode had its first free trial months after launch, in the game's third season. That said, Endgame continued to be freely available until Season 6.

The DMZ trial also coincides with the launch of Modern Warfare 4's iteration of free-to-play Call of Duty battle royale mode Warzone, and Season 1. Indeed, both DMZ and the new Warzone take place on the same Hajin map, so even if you don't decide to buy the full game to continue playing DMZ, some of that map knowledge will certainly transfer to Warzone.

The DMZ trial does not appear to have any limits, meaning you can climb the ranks, access Story Missions - the only way to play PvE, with caveats - and complete Orders to your heart's content. That includes X01, the new endgame dungeon-like area available to experienced and fully-equipped players.

DMZ players who've been asking Infinity Ward to offer a PvE-only playlist of the PvPvE mode will certainly be happy with the influx of new players, as they could potentially amplify their calls for a PvP-free playlist.

#3919. GTA 5 art director: "Let what's best for the game dictate the way forward"

Aaron Garbut explains what Rockstar learned to help shape GTA 5

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 studio head Aaron Garbut said that the most valuable lesson Rockstar learned ahead of GTA 5 was to kill its darlings, and "let what's best for the game dictate the way forward."

Speaking to Edge magazine back in 2013, Aaron Garbut, who served as art director on GTA 5, was asked what the most valuable lessons Rockstar had learned from earlier Grand Theft Auto games had been. In response, he said that it was "mostly not to get locked down to anything, whether it's a process, a plan, a goal, an asset, an idea - anything."

Garbut said the key was "to keep completely open-minded, adapt to the situation and always look for a better way forward, rather than stick with what's been decided previously. I don't mean chop and change for the sake of it, but let what's best for the game dictate the way forward. With a game that's as large and complex as this, the ideas need to be fluid, and you need to be paying as much attention as you can to every aspect to make sure they're working together."

His philosophy isn't exactly a brand-new one. The idea of killing your darlings - abandoning even your very favorite ideas if you find they no longer actually serve the project you're working on - has long been touted across the entire artistic industry. But applied to the complexity of a game like GTA 5, and its then-industry-leading open-world, the idea of knowing when to move on takes on increased importance.

Even back in 2013, Garbut acknowledged that Rockstar was lucky to have an art team "that is extremely experienced at building open worlds," and was rarely stumped by brand-new problems. Even so, "there's always new things that come along [...] and the nature of how we approach development means that we need to be ready to adapt." For Rockstar, that's a layering approach, where the world is built first, and then missions, story, and game structure are added on top. "Each of these things influences the others massively," Garbut said, "so each needs to adapt to the others. We are always playing and refining, adjusting each element of the game to play better with the others."

That approach puts Rockstar in a spot where even when it does do away with ideas that aren't working "we're rarely throwing away content." Instead, plans are adapted, and the studio is "constantly looking ahead with a clean slate, rather than sticking stubornly to old decisions."

It sounds basic, but Garbut's idea here is a pivotal one in a medium as complex as game design. There's a though that few, if any, other forms of art are trying as hard to not get made as video games are, and when some ideas work well with certain features but clash with others, or take ages to actually implement (often at the expense of other systems), reworking them, or even abandoning them entirely, can be an important way to actually get projects finished on time. Sometimes that means that the grand ambitions of the developers don't get entirely delivered on, but if that means getting the game into players hands - or even avoiding having your studio shuttered around you - it's an important discipline to hone.

#3918. As The Elder Scrolls 5 turns 15, massive mod Beyond Skyrim: Bruma gets a 2.0 update delivering a new quest, extra dungeons and an "expanded worldspace"

"The reason for this update is actually a technical necessity"

Warning: I'm probably about to make you feel old. Today, November 11th 2026, is the 15th anniversary of Skyrim's release. The first one, before it was re-released on every other platform under the sun. Fittingly, one of its best expansion mods, Beyond Skyrim: Bruma, has gotten a beefy 2.0 update to commemorate the occasion. Though, its creators insist the main driving force behind the update was more a matter of "technical necessity". There are new quests, dungeons, and corners of Skyrim-era Cyrodiil to explore either way.

"You might ask yourself why, after all these years, we have put any more work into polishing and even adding new content to Bruma," the Beyond Skyrim team wrote in an article about the making of their version of Bruma's 2.0 update. "We are, of course, working on the whole province of Cyrodiil, and have made significant progress which you can follow on our social media. With so much still to go however, it was not out of nostalgia for a 15 year old Skyrim or a nearly 10 year old Bruma that we decided to revisit the first, and as of the time of writing, only major Beyond Skyrim release.

"The reason for this update is actually a technical necessity," the modders continued. "The problem we have with Bruma is that it is based on a very very old version of Cyrodiil, which had been branched off of the main development build of Cyrodiil soon after Bruma's initial release in 2017. Whenever we updated Bruma, that meant we had to merge our changes into two builds, the public Bruma build and the WIP Cyrodiil build." So, in order to solve that behind-the-scenes problem, the team have developed a "build stripper" tool which means they'll not have to juggle maintaining two builds going forwards.

As laid out in the showcase video above, the modders have also used Bruma 2.0 as an opportunity to overhaul and add to vast chunks of their recreation of Cyrodiil's northernmost county. A fully voiced quest called All The Wrong Places which was cut from the mod's initial release, "several new dungeons and interiors", and an expansion of the explorable area all grace the changelog.

More clothing, armour, weapons including the mod's first spear, enemies, spells, enchantments, world encounters, books, and treasure maps have also been shipped in with the 2.0 version, alongside overhauls to boss fights. A new opening title splash will greet you upon entering Bruma for the first time, you should benefit from higher FPS as you explore the city, and the modders have even added an apple to Jerall View Inn. That's far from the end of the tweaks, so it's well worth reading the full list if you've got time.

"All in all, Bruma 2.0 has been a massive journey, one where we have built and learned a lot, and most importantly, made many advancements to prepare us for the future," the modders concluded. If you've not given Beyond Skyrim: Bruma a go, I can very much recommend it. You might find yourself wandering back across the border into Skyrim once you've had your fill of nostalgia-tinged exploration and staring at a distant Imperial City you can't visit, but the original version's still good for hours of extra Elder Scrollsing.

You can grab the 2.0 version of Beyond Skyrim: Bruma from Nexus Mods. It's worth noting that you'll need "a recent version (1.6 or higher) of Skyrim: Special Edition's update.esm and update.bsa" and a separate mod containing Beyond Skyrim's shared asset repository. Saves made using previous versions of Beyond Skyrim: Bruma won't work with the 2.0 update, so it's likely worth starting a new playthrough or relying on an in-progress one you've yet to use any mods with.

#3917. The Outer Worlds 2's first story expansion could well be the opening to the series' last hurrah and will have you hunting for a cure to "explosive cell death" in December

Sub Rosa sci-fi drama and a new region to explore await

Since they released The Outer Worlds 2 around this time last year, the world has rather turned upside down for Obsidian. The studio lost a chunk of staff to Microsoft's mass layoffs and have pivoted to making a new Fallout game as a smaller group shoved underneath Bethesda in Xbox's corporate structure.

Given all that, The Outer Worlds 2's two-part story expansion is likely arriving in vastly different circumstances than those the studio might've imagined when they began sketching out DLC plans. Part one of the expansion, dubbed Side Effects Guaranteed, is set to release early next month.

'Oof, that looks a lot like it's been given what could turn out to be a death spot parked right in the aftermath of GTA 6's initial launch on consoles' is what I thought when I first saw that Side Effects Guaranteed's launch date is December 2nd. That said, Obsidian have also made clear that a second DLC in the two-part narrative expansion to the sci-fi RPG is set to follow in spring 2027. So if this does turn out to be the end of the series, with a third Outer Worlds game currently looking very unlikely following the substantial upheaval I mentioned in the intro, at least it won't risk being totally obscured by a Rockstar crime game-shaped eclipse.

As for what this first dose of extra Outer Worlds 2 has in store for December, Obsidian summed it up as follows:

As you pursue the cure and set course for Elysium, an area home to former subjects of base game authoritarian collectivist faction the Protectorate, you'll be faced with the choice of whether to side with Gordon Hazen or Algernon Lankester. Both are agents of black market smuggling organisation Sub Rosa, with one sounding like the goody-two-shoes diplomatic type and the other wanting to "exploit the subjects for his own personal gain". Sounds more Saturday morning cartoon than serious RPG story with serious choices, but that's always tended to be how The Outer Worlds leans.

Rounding out the expansion are new enemies, gear, flaws which give your character build a funky twist, and a bumping up of the level cap from from 30 to 36. Fittingly given I'm writing this on Skyrim's 15th birthday, one of the new flaws is named 'Must Have Been the Wind' after the meme of enemies in the likes of Bethesda and Obsidian's games returning to chill mode after being shot in the face with an arrow or facing some other obvious sign they're under attack. To encourage folks to dive back in, The Outer Worlds 2 is getting options to respec your character's skills and edit how many skill points are dished out per level up via an update alongside Side Effects Guaranteed.

As much as I'm resigned to the series' likely fate as Obsidian return to Fallout and won't pretend The Outer Worlds 2 was great rather than good, I'm still hopeful it can go out with a bang in these two expansions, if indeed this is the studio's last trip to space for the foreseeable future. It's worth noting that if you bought The Outer Worlds 2's premium edition, these expansions are included as part of it and so will come to you at no extra cost.

#3916. GTA 6 reportedly has 55 Achievements/Trophies, more than both GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 had at launch

GTA 6 is due to release on the 19th November on PS5, and Xbox Series X/S, and ahead of the highly-anticipated launch of Rockstar's latest sandbox adventure, people just can't get enough information about the game. To that end, overnight, we saw our latest leak: the game will have 55 Trophies/Achievements.

In a now-deleted tweet from (in)famous Rockstar dataminer, TexFunz2 - re-posted by the Twitter account iGrandTheftAuto - it appears the game will have 55 individual rewards for completing certain tasks and missions. At the time of writing, we don't know specifically what these challenges are, but it seems none of them will be attached to the online version of the game; the base game launches without GTA Online, and so we can safely assume that all these rewards will be for the single-player only content. GTA Online will drop sometime in 2027, according to Twitch's CEO.

If you've been paying attention to previous Rockstar titles, you'll know that Grand Theft Auto 5 launched with 51 Achievements/Trophies - again, all single-player - and Red Dead Redemption 2 launched with 52. So the latest game has more than either game got at launch - and I can tell you from experience, getting Platinum in either title was a very time-consuming experience. Expect the same to be true here, too.

It's worth highlighting that GTA 5 did, eventually, get more Achievements and Trophies: the GTA Online content upped the complete total to 78, adding 27 new challenges to complete. I would expect GTA 6 to do the same… whenever the PC version of GTA comes out, or GTA Online lands in the new game (it's possible both could happen at the same time).

Recently, we heard why a former Rockstar Games tech director thinks GTA 6 could be coming to PC sooner than you'd expect (mostly thanks to AI clones), when we can expect the pre-load of the game (10th November), and how big the final game install is expected to be (210GB). The final game is expected to be so big and dense with detail that no single Rockstar employee has seen the entire game, meaning there are plenty of easter eggs and ridiculous things to discover.

#3915. Guide: Who Is the GTA 6 Cover Art Girl and Is She Based on a Real Person?

What we know about the GTA 6 cover art girl so far

GTA 6 is going live now worldwide, and that means you might have more questions about the cover girl on the box art. In this GTA 6 guide, we're covering who is the GTA 6 cover art girl and is she based on a real person?

On this page: Who Is the GTA 6 Cover Art Girl and Is She Based on a Real Person?

With GTA 6 now available, we'll be able to find out if the cover art girl actually appears in the game. Up until now, Rockstar hasn't commented on who she is.

At the time of writing, with the game going live worldwide, there hasn't been any evidence of the GTA 6 cover girl being found in the game.

GTA games have often had women on their box arts, but it's important to note this doesn't necessarily mean they'll play an important role in the story — or even appear at all. History has taught us the girls on the front cover can sometimes appear in minor roles within the plot, but they're usually not critical to the story.

For example, the cover girl from GTA 5, the girl taking a picture in a red bikini, doesn't appear in the game whatsoever. It is the same for GTA 4: the girl wearing a red top and licking a lollipop isn't in the game. In fact, in terms of the mainline entries, you'd need to go back to Vice City for an example of the cover girl actually being in the game.

As such, there's a chance the GTA 6 cover girl is purely for promotional purposes — she might not be in the game at all.

So, there's a fairly good chance the GTA 6 cover girl won't be in the game itself, but is she based on a real person? While developer Rockstar hasn't said yet, the Internet believes it's found someone with a very, very strong resemblance.

Gabriela Chiquin, who is an influencer, DJ, and musician from Venezuela, looks a lot like the GTA 6 cover girl. In a number of Instagram posts, she has her hair curled similarly to the cover girl, and wears green clothing. The pictures of her in green are from a few years ago, so they weren't taken in response to the attention she's gotten from the link to GTA 6.

Having caught wind of the similarities, she said in an Instagram post: "I want to thank the entire GTA community for so much love. I never imagined receiving so many messages, comments, and memes." She doesn't actually say whether she is the GTA 6 cover girl or not, however.

The cover girls for its game isn't something Rockstar usually makes a big deal out of, so it's unlikely we'll ever get official confirmation that Chiquin is the actual inspiration for the GTA 6 cover girl. Still, there's a very clear resemblance here, and the Internet managed to make the connection within days.

The Final Fantasy 14 community might still be a good few months away from new expansion Evercold, but Square Enix is keeping us on our toes with its "longest" free login period ever – and a, uh, new optional $18 purchase folks can't get enough of.

Fans first datamined the jirai-kei-inspired outfit back in April, seeing screenshots go viral and eager players questioning when developers might finally add it to the MMO. Well, it's been a solid seven months now, and it's finally available to purchase on the Mog Station – for nearly 20 bucks, that is. And, the outfit, aptly dubbed the "Alternative Dress Attire," fit with its frilly blouse and short skirt combo, is once again making rounds online.

Why, you might ask? One person sums it up perfectly over on Reddit, writing, "The latest mass-production Limsa e-girl outfit has arrived," screenshot of their Au Ra donning the new drip. Another poster shares a similar image, saying, "The new dress truly is exquisite." The comments see fans exclaim "it dyes so well, too" – and I can happily personally confirm that, indeed, it does dye very well (pastel pink, my beloved…).

It’s here! 💕 Achieve the apex of style with the Alternative Dress Attire, now available on the FFXIV Online Store! 🎀 https://t.co/I0a0LY57jb https://t.co/bgaFQhrPeMNovember 16, 2026

Responses under the official Final Fantasy 14 account's own thread on Twitter are just as positive – and amusing, of course. One player says they "couldn't resist" buying the outfit, while another jests, "Cat girls 'bout to set records on this one." And they're probably not wrong. Log in and head to the game's ever-controversial roleplay and idling hub to see for yourself.

Will all the cat, dragon, and elf girlies now be taking on Kefka in UMAD in their cutesy new skirts? I know that I certainly will. I just can't wait to see what the community comes up with in terms of creative mixing and matching for glams with this set, honestly. It's bound to absolutely dominate the Eorzea Collection, I'd wager – and hopefully inspire Square Enix to introduce more real-life fashion-adjacent purchases to its optional store.

#3913. Dungeons in World of Warcraft: Forever get a huge XP buff, but power-levellers shouldn't celebrate just yet

World of Warcraft: Forever has received a massive buff to the XP drop-rates of dungeon mobs (enemies), which should make running these instances multiple times feel more rewarding - and may revive an older levelling strategy.

This buff is a 50 percent increase in experience from all mobs killed inside all dungeons. As detailed in this World of Warcraft forum post, community manager Kaivax wrote that this change has been made "so it feels better to go back in for more runs". They don't outright say this is in response to community feedback, but the subject has been a hot topic since the beta.

World of Warcraft: Forever developers have spoken in the past about the decision to deliberately bring down dungeon mob XP to disincentivise power-levelling in dungeons. The idea was that by doing this, people would be encouraged to actually go out into the world and explore it, rather than hopping from instance to instance until they reached max level.

Sadly, a side effect of this change is that doing a dungeon more than once could feel unrewarding. Playing it once is great, as you get to complete lots of quests that reward guaranteed items and XP. However, if you go back again, you don't get these, so your only source of progression comes from a heavily decreased XP rate.

Some quests exacerbate this issue. Dungeons like Wailing Caverns and especially Blackfathom Deeps have a quest that can't really be completed in one run due to a reliance on drop rates for items you need, and having to fight for drops with the rest of your dungeon party. Having to go back to complete this used to suck, and now it sucks less!

So does this mean farming dungeons to power-level is back? Maybe, but it still won't be nearly as efficient as it was in older versions of Classic WoW. The current mob XP rates, after this buff, will still only be 36 percent of the original Classic rate - a third. Given how fast you can level by doing quests out in the world, it seems dungeon farming isn't due for a comeback just yet.

After an especially smooth launch, World of Warcraft: Forever has become the biggest launch in the series' history, beating out Wrath of the Lich King, Cataclysm, and all the other past expansion launches. The developers have been quick to hotfix things on the fly, including a change that left PvP battlegrounds heavily advantaged for the Horde.

#3912. Lootboxes, pay-to-win, virtual currencies and other blights unto gaming face heavy regulation as the EU tables new Digital Fairness Act

It's been 10 years since I lasted opened a lootbox, I think. Just thought you should know.

Loot boxes, dark patterns, virtual currencies, subscription services, pay-to-win systems, and many other trappings of diabolical digital serfdom all face extensive regulation under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act, which has been formally presented to EU member states today. The full draft text of the regulation leaked earlier in the week. If it passes into law - and there's plenty of debate and revision ahead - it'll have big consequences for the developers and publishers of games like Overwatch, Dota 2, and GTA Online.

You can now read the draft text here on the EU Commission's official site. The organisers have also published an introductory explainer that takes us through the timeline of the Act's gestation, dating back to 2020, and summarises its provisions. If passed, the Act will apply to any company doing business in the EU, not just those based in member states, with individual governments able to impose fines and consumers able to seek financial compensation if they think they've been harmed.

Here's a summary from me, based on a quick delve through the text. The Act proposes a number of provisions regarding "unfair" commercial practices, including omission and distortion in advertising and PR communication at large. Amongst other things, it takes aim at "dark patterns" – that is, "visual, auditory and other components" of online interfaces that are designed to manipulate or deceive. The text also forbids personalised advertising and pricing aimed at children, and prohibits influencers from making "direct exhortations to minors to buy products or to persuade their parents or other adults to buy products in commercial communications".

The items that are probably of greatest interest to us smelly gamers are the passages on virtual currencies, "variable reward systems", and addictive design.

The Act would require game publishers who sell virtual currencies to indicate the real-world monetary value of the currency and anything bought with it. It would also require companies to disable paid-for virtual currencies by default for kids, unless a parent or guardian has given approval.

As for paid-for "variable reward systems", aka "loot boxes", "surprise mechanics", "Schrödinger's Giftbombs" or however publishers may prefer to describe them, the Act would require companies to state the "types" of object they might cough up, together with the probability of obtaining them. It would also oblige publishers to disable paid-for "variable reward systems" for minors, and give everybody an "easily accessible" way to switch them off.

The draft Act outright prohibits "pay-to-progress and pay-to-win mechanisms" for kids. More generally, it suggests further constraints for publishers and developers who "design, organise or operate their digital products in a manner that is intended, or can reasonably be foreseen to encourage compulsive or excessive use". Again, it wants companies to give people options to switch these features off.

That includes "features enabling automatic play of content and uninterrupted content consumption without effective and regular interruption moments that enable deliberation by the consumer on their willingness to consume more content". Also, "notifications not triggered by, or not directly related to, the consumer’s interaction or activity on the service", "features incentivising engagement at regular times or with greater frequency, including through penalties or loss of benefits", and "features and system behaviours that encourage continued use by simulating interpersonal relations," such as nagging prompts.

If you'd like a more 'expert' account of the Digital Fairness Act - how dare you! I have read several Wikipedia pages - the bespectacled nabobs of GamesIndustry.biz went and got notes from an actual lawyer. All this follows a change in EU rating law last month aimed at safeguarding the weans from predatory habit-forming devices and instruments of financialisation - games with lootboxes are now PEGI 16 by default, while blockchain games are always rated 18. Across the pond, meanwhile, lawsuits are underway in New York and Washington against Valve's tolerance of lootboxes on Steam, which the lawyers in question define as illegal gambling.

#3911. London department store Selfridges launches sizeable GTA 6 takeover, featuring a varsity jacket that costs an eye-watering £2,500

Expensive British department store Selfridges has launched a sizeable Grand Theft Auto 6 takeover, completely making-over its Oxford Street London Corner Shop store and offering a considerable line of clothing, which includes an exclusive varsity jacket that costs a bank-melting £2,500. Note, you can buy the GTA 6 items online as well.

Live from Selfridges at Oxford Street for the #GTAVI activation🌴Rockstar are not messing around 🤯 pic.twitter.com/vqqXKwB1oJ

That GTA 6 varsity jacket is by far and away the most expensive item (and it's apparently already sold out), next to a non-exclusive varsity jacket that's £1,750, whereas the other items are pricey but conceivably affordable.

There are a few ranges on offer. There's a nice bright teal and pink-coloured range based around the spoof NFL team the Vice City Manatees, which includes a manatee plushie, an American football, a jacket, and other bits and bobs. There's also a range based around the spoof NBA team, the Vice City Narcos, that includes a basketball (there's a standard GTA 6-branded basketball too).

There's a range based on the spoof fast-food chain Burger Shot, which includes a visor, work uniform, and apron, amusingly. There are some admirably horrid postcard-decorated shirts and shorts, and there's a lot of generic game-branded caps and T-shirts besides, all in quite nice colours. Quirky branded offerings include an ashtray, money clip and dartboard. It's all quite attractive stuff.

There's no word on how long the items will be stocked for or that the Selfridges Corner Shop takeover will run for, other than "while stocks last".

Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives 19th November - next week - so the hype machine is now in full effect. GTA 6 pre-load dates, times and details have been announced, and we know what the GTA 6 Trophies and Achievements will be.

#3910. "Some of the best games of the last decade came from teams of fifty": Destroy All Humans! remake devs Black Forest Games split from THQ Nordic to launch new indie studio group

"We're excited to shape our own future as owners again"

Black Forest Games, developers of the Destroy All Humans! remakes, have spun out of Embracer Group-owned publishers THQ Nordic via a management buyout and announced plans to form a new "developer-driven group" of independent studios. The new group, dubbed Third Signal, will aim to "give teams the independence, resources and creative freedom" to "bring their own ideas to life".

Black Forest, based in Germany, announced the move in a press release. "We are grateful to THQ Nordic and Embracer for nine good years and the games we made together," co-boss Adrian Goersch said. "Now, we're excited to shape our own future as owners again, to work on an exciting new project with a great team and strong partners behind us."

Black Forest had been in the embrace since 2017, releasing both 2020's Destroy All Humans! remake and Destroy All Humans! 2: Reprobed in that time, plus DLC Clone Carnage. Over the years they've also made multiple entries in the Giana Sisters platformer series, survival game Fade to Silence, and 2017's Bubsy: The Woolies Strike Back.

That's a right old mix of stuff, but the biggest names in it are all resurrections of series or characters created by other folks back in the day. Pandemic Studios in the case of Destroy All Humans!, Accolade in the case of Bubsy, and Germany company Time Warp in the case of Giana Sisters. That makes the fact it sounds like this move'll give Black Forest a bit more creative freedom intriguing. Here's hoping that if they do plan to try and get some more of their own original ideas off the ground, rather than trucking on with a steady diet of remakes and revivals, they manage to stick the landing. It's all fine declaring that a 50 person team can make a top game these days, but that certainly doesn't mean it's in any way easy to pull off.

#3909. Clair Obscur Studio Has Lost One of Its Most Important Developers

Jennifer Svedberg-Yen was the narrative lead on Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. She basically shaped the game's twisting and turning story, which many would argue is its greatest asset.

And so it's a bit of a gut punch to hear that she actually left developer Sandfall Interactive earlier this year — meaning that, unless she's already helped establish some of the project's narrative groundwork, she won't be involved with the studio's next game.

Svedberg-Yen dropped this bombshell in an interview with Gamesbeat, having just won a 'Breakthrough US' award at the BAFTAs for her work on Clair Obscur.

"I left Sandfall in July, after wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition. We’ve parted ways," she explains.

It should be stressed that Svedberg-Yen really did spearhead the Game of the Year-winning title's story and tone right from the start; it wouldn't have been the experience that it was without her.

"I was the third person on the team. The team didn’t exist, actually. When I joined it was two guys who were still working at Ubisoft," she explains.

"The studio didn’t exist. It was the two co-founders and then me. Then we brought in the composer, and then the art director. Several months later we brought in the third co-founder, and then several months after that started the studio. So I was one of the founding members of the team."

Svedberg-Yen continues: "We came up with the idea together from the very start. It was always, from the very beginning, a narrative-focused game. It’s a narrative-first game. That’s what the creative director always said as well. Narrative is king."

And that approach is clear to see in the finished product, which has been lauded for its plot and characters ever since its release back in April of last year.

Svedberg-Yen goes on to talk about how important it is to establish narrative cohesion right off the bat, so that the whole development cycle is built around one vision. She thinks that too many games see story as something that can be slotted in over time, or simply added later on — and the whole thing suffers for it.

As for her own creative process, Svedberg-Yen provides some interesting insight: "I don’t think I could have written something like Expedition in my 20s, or even my 30s."

"I very much believe that one of the most powerful things we can do to train our ability to tell a good story is actually to live a rich life, to observe others, to learn how people work. If you’re trying to write about people, you must understand people."

Svedberg-Yen intends to work on her own projects going forward, which includes writing for film and TV — but she's also passionate about promoting the importance of narrative in video games.

As such, she wants to set up some kind of initiative, helping narrative-focused creatives make the next step in getting their games funded, and in turn, reshape the wider industry's perspective when it comes to storytelling. Sounds like a pretty noble goal to me.

Still, with everything Clair Obscur achieved in terms of narrative, you'd think that Svedberg-Yen will be difficult to replace.

We know that Sandfall Interactive is in the very early stages of developing its next title, but beyond vague, teasing statements, nothing has been made official just yet.

What do you make of this departure? What did you think of Clair Obscur's narrative? Ponder what comes next in the comments section below.

#3908. "Art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI" Bandai Namco and Monolith Soft helped out with Ocarina of Time on Switch 2

Xenoblade series developer Monolith Soft and Bandai Namco Studios have been listed as support studios for the Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time, working on elements of the title such as "art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI". Special thanks to both companies appear in the credits for the newly-launched game (as you can see below) and a statement released by Bandai Namco Studios confirms its involvement, too.

"We were commissioned to produce some of the visual assets and artwork, including characters, environments, animations, cutscenes, and UI elements, for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a Nintendo Switch 2 game released by Nintendo Co., Ltd. on 5th November, 2026," reads a translated release from Bandai Namco Studio reads.

Of course, this isn't the first time we've seen Bandai Namco Studios' talents leveraged to help with Nintendo games: the publisher and its internal studios worked closely with Nintendo as a co-developer on the long-awaited Metroid Prime 4, and we know the studios are listed as co-developer for first-party Switch 2 titles like Mario Kart World and Splatoon Raiders. Typically, the work carried out by Bandai Namco comes from one of two dedicated internal studios that are contracted specifically to work with Nintendo: Studio 2 and Studio S. You can see a full list of the games Bandai Namco's support studios have worked on here. You'll note there are many Nintendo first-party titles listed here, going back to 2012 and Mario Kart 8. In late 2025, Nintendo acquired Bandai Namco Studios Singapore from the publisher, renaming the company Nintendo Studios Singapore.

"Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve," wrote our reviewer, Christian Donlan, in his five-star review of the Switch 2 game last week. "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

If - somehow! - you've already gobbled up most of the game and you're keen to play it again, you will be pleased to know that Master Quest code has been found in datamined files for the title, suggesting DLC may well be on the way in the not-too-distant future.

"My first layoff in 14 years making games"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update: Following the publication of this story, Crystal Dynamics reached out with the following statement.

"Crystal Dynamics made a difficult, but necessary business decision to reduce our current studio staff by 8 people. Whenever we phase roles off a project, we make every effort to find new spots for our great colleagues first. Everyone affected receives a full severance package as well as job placement assistance to aid them through this transition. We wish them the best and hope to work together in the future."

Original story: Yet another round of layoffs has apparently gone down at Tomb Raider studio Crystal Dynamics, as developers report that they've been cut from the studio. This is at least the sixth round of layoffs since the studio last shipped an original game.

Multiple developers have posted on LinkedIn about the layoffs, as reported by Vertical Slice. Those include UI software engineer Garin R. K. Richards and senior game designer Joshua Mitchell. "After several rounds of layoffs at Crystal Dynamics, today it was my turn," Mitchell writes. "My first layoff in 14 years making games."

Also cut is senior environment technical artist Kevin Baker, who led the development of "procedural tools used extensively in the creation of Tomb Raider: Catalyst's game world," and "integrated Claude Code into procedural tool development." We already knew that Legacy of Atlantis is being made with AI, and it seems the studio is keen to use similar generative tech in Catalyst – though not keen enough to keep the people responsible for it employed, I guess.

Crystal Dynamics has not shipped a new game since the release of Marvel's Avengers in 2020. Since then, it was acquired by Embracer Group, a parent company that's undergone no shortage of financial upheaval in recent years. In 2023, Embracer insisted that Crystal Dynamics would be unaffected by the ongoing layoffs at the broader company, a few months before laying off people at the Tomb Raider studio.

Counting today's cuts, there have been five more rounds of layoffs since then. There were three sets of cuts in 2025 alone, both before and after Perfect Dark – which Crystal Dynamics had been co-developing – was cancelled at Xbox. The studio insisted it was still "fully committed" to its upcoming Tomb Raider games when it announced yet more layoffs in March 2026.
